name: A Pilgrim's Copper Petition
description: An old copper coin, green at the edges, with a folded square of rice-paper tied to it by a waxed thread. The paper, unfolded a finger's width, asks the Founder's Stone for a blessing on the soil of a farm the pilgrim has not returned to in eleven years. The coin is to be set at the stone; the paper is for the register's question-column, which few gatekeepers still keep. The pilgrim walked up from the foothills at second hour, set the coin on the gate-step, bowed, and walked down again without waking anyone. The copper is warm with having been held.

name: A Courier's Valley Slip
description: A narrow strip of grey silk folded three times and sealed with a single pressed thumbprint in cinnabar — the Thousand Venom Valley's small seal, not the Matriarch's large one. A courier came up from the south at fourth hour wearing a wet gorge-cloak, handed the slip across the register without crossing the threshold, and walked back into the dark. The slip is addressed to Elder Baixu; it is not for reading. Chen left it on the register under a stone weight, for the morning steward to carry in.

name: A Mother's Unanswered Question
description: A piece of paper folded once, and then smoothed flat again, and then folded once more, by a hand that kept forgetting it had already folded it. The question, written in the careful characters of a woman who does not write often, asks whether a man named Shen Rongzhi came up this road eight winters past — thin, left-handed, a scar below the right ear. The paper is to be left in the gate-register's question-column. The woman came up from the Crossing at sixth hour and would not be persuaded to wait for Elder Baixu. She did not give her own name.

name: Chen's Stroke-Pin
description: A small bronze pin the length of a thumbnail, shaped like the single brush-stroke a careful archivist uses to distinguish *chen* — the morning — from *cheng* — a name the Azure Cloud no longer reads aloud. Gatekeeper Chen pressed the pin into your hand without meeting your eye, after Librarian Zhao corrected the stroke in the gate-register. 'I cannot wear it,' he said. 'It is mine, and I cannot wear it. The sect will not know why I am wearing what I am. You will know, and that is better.' The pin has the small, unshowy weight of a thing that was not supposed to be given.

name: The Outer Disciple's Broom
description: A pale-straw broom bound to a shaft of worn paulownia, its handle darkened at the grip where a single pair of hands has held it for six weeks of watches. Gatekeeper Chen — Inner Disciple Chen, now, though the courtyard will take a month to say it right — set the broom across both palms and offered it to you at dawn, on the morning of his second trial. He did not say thank you. He said, 'The gate-register's second column has your name under warm ink. This belongs there too, but I am not ready to set it in the rafters yet.' Held right — the way an outer disciple holds a broom, which is to say the way a sword is held before the hand has earned a sword — the paulownia is a staff that parries as well as strikes, and the courtesy of its weight is that it does not ask more of the arm than the arm offers.
